lesson.text: An argument has a claim supported by reasons and evidence. Strong arguments use relevant, sufficient evidence.
Irrelevant evidence doesn't support the claim, even if it is true: "School uniforms save time, and our school was built in 1990."
Watch for tricks: attacking a person instead of their idea, claiming "everyone agrees", or offering only two choices when there are more.
To evaluate an argument, find each piece of evidence and ask whether it truly supports the claim.

exercises.prompt: True evidence can still be irrelevant to a claim.
Which evidence is irrelevant to "Uniforms save time"?
choices: Pupils spend less time choosing clothes.
exercises.explain: The school's age has nothing to do with saving time.

exercises.prompt: "Everyone agrees, so it must be true." What is wrong?
exercises.explain: Many people agreeing doesn't prove it.

exercises.prompt: Attacking a person instead of their idea is a weak argument.
"We must ban phones or pupils will fail." What trick is this?
choices: only two choices when there are more
exercises.explain: It pretends there are only two choices.

exercises.prompt: Claim: "Reading daily helps vocabulary." Which evidence is most relevant?
choices: A study found daily readers knew more words.
exercises.explain: The study directly supports the claim.

exercises.prompt: "Don't listen to her plan; she's always late." What is wrong?
choices: It attacks the person, not the plan.
exercises.explain: Being late says nothing about the plan.

exercises.prompt: A strong argument needs enough evidence, not just one example.
Which question best tests a piece of evidence?
choices: Does this really support the claim?
exercises.explain: Ask whether it supports the claim.

exercises.prompt: An article claims bikes cut pollution. It cites cleaner air after bike lanes, and a cyclist's favourite song. Which doesn't belong?
exercises.explain: The song has nothing to do with pollution.

exercises.prompt: Why might a writer include irrelevant evidence?
choices: to seem convincing without real support
exercises.explain: Extra evidence can look impressive without proving anything.

exercises.prompt: Claim: "Our team is the best." Evidence: "We have the newest kit." Why is this weak?
exercises.explain: Kit says nothing about how well they play.

exercises.prompt: Removing irrelevant evidence can make an argument clearer.
Order the steps to evaluate an argument.
items: Judge if what remains is enough.
